teaser: A palace is being butchered, and the man who gave the order rests on his elbow and watches.
review_notes:
Dimensions about 392 x 496 cm (Louvre).
Shown at the Salon of 1827-28; Delacroix's own catalog note describing the scene (Aischeh hanging herself, Baleah the cupbearer).
Sosthene de La Rochefoucauld's warning to Delacroix to change his manner: per Delacroix's letters.
“Massacre no. 2” nickname by Delacroix.
Sold to John Wilson in 1846; bought by the Louvre in 1921.
Byron's play (1821) has no massacre: the slaughter is Delacroix's addition.
Use of pastel studies for the picture.
Identification of the upper figure with raised arms as Aischeh is the usual reading.

lesson.text: Everything in this picture is screaming except its main character. Women are stabbed, a horse is dragged in to be killed, smoke rolls toward the bed. And at the top of the heap a bearded man in white props his head on his hand, as if he were a little bored at the theater.

He is Sardanapalus, a legendary king of ancient Assyria. In the story his city is besieged and about to fall. Rather than let his enemies take anything he has enjoyed, he piles his treasures on a huge pyre, the heap of wood on which he himself will burn, and orders that his women, his pages, even his horses and dogs be killed in front of him.

Delacroix was twenty-nine when he showed this at the Paris Salon, the big official exhibition, in the winter of 1827 to 1828. He found the subject in a play by the English poet Lord Byron, the idol of young Romantics. Byron's king dies nobly with one faithful companion. The massacre is Delacroix's own invention.

lesson.title: Calm and carnage
lesson.text: Start with the king, then follow what his order sets in motion.

spots.title: The king
spots.text: Head on his fist, eyes dark and far away. He is painted in cool whites while everything around him burns red. He does not lift a finger.

spots.title: At his feet
spots.text: A woman has thrown herself across the bed, arms spread, face buried in the cover. She is usually seen as Myrrha, his favorite. He does not look down at her.

spots.title: The killing
spots.text: A guard pulls a woman back against him and drives a dagger toward her throat. Her body arches in a long pale curve, the brightest flesh in the picture.

spots.title: The horse
spots.text: A servant hauls the king's white horse toward the pyre by its red reins. Its eye rolls with terror under a harness loaded with gold and pearls.

lesson.text: The cruelty is deliberate, and so is the beauty. Delacroix paints the jewels, the silks and the skin with obvious delight, and that is exactly what horrified people. The picture does not tell you whom to pity or what lesson to draw.

Delacroix himself called the painting his “Massacre number two.” Number one was “The Massacre at Chios,” shown three years earlier, which at least had real victims of a real war to justify its violence.

The canvas is enormous: nearly 4 meters high and 5 wide (about 13 by 16 feet). You would expect something that large to be built on a stable frame of verticals and horizontals. Delacroix does the opposite, and the bed seems to slide toward you.
Here is the skeleton under the chaos.

lines.label: The great diagonal
lines.text: Everything pours from the king in the upper left down to the heap of bodies and treasure in the lower right, like lava running downhill.

lines.label: The red bed
lines.text: The bed is a slab of pink and scarlet tipped up at an impossible angle. No floor, no walls: there is nothing steady for the eye to stand on.

lines.label: The king's line of sight
lines.text: His gaze runs along the same slope, down toward the murder at the right. He is the only spectator who gets a comfortable seat.

lesson.text: Classical painting asked for clear drawing, balance and a moral. Delacroix answered with color, movement and feeling. That choice is the heart of Romanticism, the movement that put emotion ahead of rules.

The reaction was brutal. Critics called it confused, badly drawn, a painter's mistake. Even admirers were uneasy. The official in charge of the fine arts summoned Delacroix and warned him to change his style if he wanted any more work from the government.
For a while the threat held. Delacroix later wrote that after this painting he went years without a public commission. The state had bought his earlier Salon pictures. It did not buy this one.
Among the wreckage Delacroix scattered objects painted with the care of a jeweler. One of them is part of the furniture, and it is an animal.
The royal bed has a beast carved into it. Can you find its head?

spots.title: The golden elephant
spots.text: An elephant's head in gold, trunk curled and jewels hanging from its brow, forms the foot of the bed. Delacroix had never seen Assyria. He assembled his East from prints, Indian and Persian objects, and imagination.

lesson.text: That mix of sources is typical. In 1827 no Assyrian palace had been dug up yet, so nobody knew what one looked like. The turbans, the ewers and the elephant belong to a dreamed Orient, the vague, luxurious East that French artists pictured long before they traveled there.

spots.title: The cupbearer
spots.text: At the far left a servant brings a golden ewer and cup on a tray. In Delacroix's own note this is the poison prepared for the king, who will die last.

spots.title: Raised arms
spots.text: A woman at the top stretches up toward a cord. Delacroix wrote that one of the women, Aischeh, hangs herself to avoid being killed by a slave.

spots.title: The plea
spots.text: A man leans in from the right edge with his hand lifted, begging the king or shielding his eyes. Nobody answers him.

spots.title: Smoke
spots.text: Gray smoke already fills the upper right corner and blurs the palace walls. The fire has started; the whole scene has minutes left.

spots.title: The treasure
spots.text: Vases, a lyre, necklaces and cloth lie dumped in the foreground, painted in thick, glittering touches. All of it is fuel.

spots.title: The witness
spots.text: A woman lying against the bed looks out blankly, the only face turned toward us. Her stillness matches the king's.

lesson.text: Delacroix prepared the colors with small studies in pastel, sticks of nearly pure powdered pigment. He was testing how reds, golds and flesh tones would vibrate together before committing them to a canvas the size of a wall.

The picture went back to his studio and stayed with him for almost twenty years before he sold it. The Louvre bought it only in 1921, close to a century after the scandal. By then painters had long accepted what it proposed: that color and movement alone can carry a picture.

One puzzle remains, and it is the one you met at the start. Is the king's calm monstrous, or is it the last dignity of a man who has already lost? Delacroix never said. Stand in front of him and decide which you see.

quiz.question: What is Sardanapalus doing while his palace is destroyed?
quiz.explanation: He rests his head on his hand and looks on.

quiz.question: Where did Delacroix find the subject?
options: In a play by Lord Byron
quiz.explanation: Byron's play inspired him, though the massacre is Delacroix's own addition.

quiz.question: What main line organizes the composition?
options: A diagonal from upper left to lower right
quiz.explanation: Everything flows down from the king to the heap in the lower right.

quiz.question: How did officials react after the Salon?
options: They warned him to change his style
They bought it at once for the Louvre
quiz.explanation: The head of the fine arts told him to change if he wanted state work.

quiz.question: What animal forms part of the bed?
quiz.explanation: A golden elephant's head decorates the foot of the bed.

quiz.question: When did the Louvre buy the painting?
quiz.explanation: It entered the Louvre nearly a century after it was first shown.

facts.text: Delacroix based the palace on Assyrian ruins he had visited.
facts.explanation: No Assyrian palace had been excavated yet; he invented his East from objects, prints and imagination.

facts.text: The painting is nearly 4 meters high and 5 meters wide.
In Byron's play, the king orders the same massacre shown in the painting.
facts.explanation: Byron's king dies nobly; the slaughter was Delacroix's invention.
